structural: Every Group contains teaching slides, at least one scenario-based case study where appropriate, an interactive widget or practical activity, and an interactive quiz with feedback.
Every Content unit contains multiple Groups and one Content-level final quiz; difficult Content units add practice quizzes.
Every Lesson contains one or more Content units and a lesson-level challenge/assessment where appropriate (esp. complex lessons).
There is no fixed order of interactions inside a Group; the ordered `items` array is the order to render.
Every interaction must have a learning purpose; do not pad counts.
Final assessments test application, not just recall.
Use relatable Nigerian scenarios and documented real events where they support the learning objective.
academic: Combine Brilliant-style accessibility with textbook-level accuracy.
Intuitive definitions must preserve the essential meaning of the formal definition.
Short slides, complete understanding: one or two closely related ideas per slide; no fixed slide count.
Do not omit qualifications, assumptions or limitations - teach them progressively.
Map concepts to specific reference chapters only after the edition is confirmed; never invent chapter numbers.
production: Every slide, case study, widget, quiz and challenge has a catchy title plus a one-sentence subtitle stating its learning purpose (Module 2 rule; applied to Module 1 where present).
Fictional figures are practice examples, not benchmarks; do not present one percentage/target as right for everyone.
Privacy: never ask learners for account numbers, PINs, passwords or other credentials.
Mobile-first: one main idea per slide, short text.
Verify arithmetic, accessibility, Nigerian terminology and any product/regulation references before release.

modules.title: Money No Be Magic
modules.purpose: Help learners understand money, how the economy affects their lives, and how human behaviour influences financial decisions.
modules.content_status: Lesson 1 fully authored; Lessons 2-15 outlined (group/case/widget/quiz titles and slide topics only).

lessons.title: Wetin Money Actually Dey Do

contents.title: Why We Need Money
contents.objective: By the end of this content, learners should understand why societies use money, how barter works, why barter can be difficult, and how money makes exchange easier.

groups.title: Market Wahala - Before Money Enter the Chat
groups.objective: Understand how people exchanged goods and services before money became widely used.
groups.group_takeaway: Before money enters the transaction, people must find other ways to agree on what gets exchanged.

items.title: Imagine Money Never Exist
items.subtitle: Explore how you would get food, clothes, and transport if nobody accepted money.

body.text: Imagine waking up tomorrow and discovering that money no longer exists.
You need breakfast, but the food seller won't accept your bank transfer. The bus driver won't accept cash. Your landlord wants something you own in exchange for rent.
How would you survive?
People still need things, and people still produce things. The challenge is finding a way for everyone to exchange what they have for what they need.

items.title: Your First Move
items.subtitle: Choose how you would obtain something you need without using money.

config.prompt: You need something but nobody accepts money. What do you do?

options.label: Offer a product or service in exchange
Find someone willing to give the item away

config.follow_up_prompt: What might make your choice difficult?

items.feedback: No right or wrong. Use the answer to open the discussion on why exchange without money is hard.

items.title: Everybody Get Wetin, Everybody Need Something
items.subtitle: See how different people can have different goods, skills, and needs.

body.text: Meet three people at a local market:
Amaka needs her phone repaired. Tunde needs food. Musa needs yams.
Everyone has something useful, but usefulness alone does not guarantee a successful exchange.
The question is: how will they arrange a trade that satisfies everyone involved?

items.title: The Market Connection
items.subtitle: Match each person's needs with what another person can offer.

scenario.narrative: Amaka offers Tunde three yams for a phone repair. Tunde refuses because he already has enough food and needs money to pay for transport.

prompts.prompt: Does Amaka have something valuable?
prompts.expected_answer: Yes - the yams are valuable, but only to someone who wants them.

prompts.prompt: Why might Tunde still reject it?
prompts.expected_answer: He already has enough food; he needs transport money.

prompts.prompt: What could Amaka do next?
prompts.expected_answer: Find another partner, or find what Tunde wants. Learner selects from solutions.

items.key_takeaway: An item can be useful without being something another person currently wants.
items.interaction_mechanics: Learners select possible solutions and receive feedback explaining why each solution may or may not work.

items.title: Welcome to Barter
items.subtitle: Learn the name for exchanging goods and services directly without money.

body.text: This arrangement is called barter.
The direct exchange of goods or services for other goods or services without using money as the medium of exchange.
Examples include:

items: A farmer exchanging yams for fish.
A designer creating a logo in exchange for a haircut.
A mechanic repairing a vehicle in exchange for bags of rice.

body.text: Barter allows people to exchange value, but making the right match can be difficult.

groups.title: The Barter Trap - Why Trading Fit Stress Person
groups.objective: Discover the major difficulties of barter and understand why direct exchange can be inconvenient.

items.title: You Get Rice, But the Seller Wants Your Shoes
items.subtitle: Understand why possessing something useful does not guarantee that someone will exchange what you need for it.

body.text: You have a bag of rice. You need a pair of shoes.
The shoemaker has the shoes you want, but doesn't need rice. He needs a phone charger.
You have something useful, but it doesn't solve the shoemaker's current problem.
This is one of barter's major limitations: the people involved must find a mutually acceptable exchange.

items.title: Make the Trade Work
items.subtitle: Experiment with different exchanges to discover how difficult barter can become.

config.mechanic: Each character holds one item and wants another. Learner drags items between characters.
config.characters_spec: AUTHOR_TODO: provide 4 characters with (has, wants). Suggested: Rice holder wants shoes; Shoemaker has shoes wants phone charger; Charger seller wants rice or a service; one more partner to create a solvable chain.
config.on_fail_feedback: Explain why the recipient may not want the offered item.
config.success_condition: All four characters receive the item they want.

items.feedback: A trade succeeds only when the parties agree on what they are exchanging.

items.title: The Food Seller No Need Your Yam
items.subtitle: Explore the problem economists call the double coincidence of wants.

body.text: Suppose you have yams and want fish. For barter to work directly:

items: You must find someone who has fish.
Both of you must agree on the quantity and terms.

body.text: Economists call this requirement the double coincidence of wants.
Two people must each want what the other offers for a direct exchange to work.
The more specific people's needs become, the harder this matching process can be.

items.title: The Two-Person Problem
items.subtitle: Identify why a trade fails even when both people have something the other could use.

scenario.narrative: Chika has vegetables and wants a schoolbag. A bag seller has a schoolbag but wants shoes. A shoemaker wants vegetables but doesn't need another schoolbag.

prompts.prompt: Who has what Chika needs?
Who wants what Chika has?
Why can't Chika complete the exchange immediately?
prompts.expected_answer: The bag seller does not want vegetables - no double coincidence of wants.

items.key_takeaway: Barter can require several people and multiple exchanges before someone gets what they originally wanted.
items.follow_up: Learner proposes a sequence of exchanges: vegetables -> shoemaker for shoes -> shoes to bag seller for the schoolbag.

items.title: One Goat No Be Equal to One Pencil
items.subtitle: Discover why agreeing on the relative value of different goods can be difficult.

body.text: Imagine exchanging a goat for exercise books.
How many books should the goat be worth? What if one person believes the goat is worth twenty books while another believes it is worth ten?
Goods differ in usefulness, availability, quality, and the needs of the people exchanging them.
Without a commonly accepted way to express prices, people must negotiate the relative value of their goods repeatedly.

items.key_takeaway: Barter can make finding trading partners, agreeing on value, and completing exchanges unnecessarily complicated.

groups.title: How Money Enters the Story
groups.objective: Understand the basic role of money in solving the difficulties of direct exchange.

items.title: What If Everybody Accepted One Thing?
items.subtitle: Explore how a commonly accepted means of payment could simplify transactions.

body.text: Return to the market. Amaka wants her phone repaired. Tunde wants transport money. Musa wants yams.
Now imagine they can all accept the same form of money.
Amaka sells her yams and receives money. She uses some of it to pay Tunde. Tunde uses the money to pay for transport.
Each person can sell something to one person and use the proceeds to buy something from another. They no longer need every trading partner to want what they personally produce.

items.title: Barter Versus Money
items.subtitle: Compare how many steps it takes to complete a purchase under different exchange systems.

rounds.label: Barter
rounds.task: Find a direct exchange that satisfies each person's needs.

rounds.label: Money
rounds.task: Sell goods for money, then use the proceeds to buy what you need.

config.reflection_prompt: Which system made it easier to obtain the item you wanted, and why?

items.feedback: Compare the counts of successes and failures across both rounds and explain the difference.

items.title: Money Has Three Important Jobs
items.subtitle: Learn the three core functions that make money useful in an economy.

body.text: Money performs three major functions.
People use money to pay for goods and services.
People use money to express and compare prices.
People can hold money and use it to make purchases in the future, although inflation can reduce what it buys.
These functions explain why money is more than the physical notes or numbers displayed in a banking app. It helps people exchange, compare, and transfer purchasing power across time.

items.title: Name That Job
items.subtitle: Test whether you can identify the function money performs in everyday situations.

questions.prompt: A trader accepts ₦2,000 for a bag of rice. Which function is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Money is used to complete a purchase, which is the medium-of-exchange function.

questions.prompt: A shopper compares a ₦5,000 shirt with a ₦3,000 shirt. Which function helps the shopper compare their prices?
questions.explanation: Prices expressed in one common unit make comparison possible - unit of account.

questions.prompt: Someone keeps money today to spend next week. Which function is demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Holding money to spend later transfers purchasing power across time - store of value.

items.title: Money No Need to Be Paper
items.subtitle: Understand why money is defined by what it does, not just by its physical appearance.

body.text: Money can take different forms. Depending on the society and financial system, it may include:

items: Electronic balances used to make payments.

body.text: A bank transfer can settle a purchase even though no physical note changes hands.
The important point is that the form of money must be accepted and usable within the relevant payment system.

items.key_takeaway: Money makes exchange easier because people can use a commonly accepted means of payment instead of relying entirely on direct barter.

groups.title: Money Don Make Life Easier - But E No Be Magic
groups.objective: Understand the benefits of money without assuming that money automatically solves every economic problem.

items.title: Sell Here, Buy Anywhere
items.subtitle: Discover how money separates selling from buying.

body.text: Under barter, a farmer who wants shoes must find a shoemaker willing to accept the farmer's produce.
With money, the farmer can sell produce to a buyer and later purchase shoes from a different seller. The two transactions do not need to involve the same people.
This flexibility allows people to specialise in producing goods or services and exchange the results for other things they need.

items.title: The Student Designer
items.subtitle: Examine how money helps someone exchange a specialised skill for everyday necessities.

scenario.narrative: Zainab designs posters for small businesses. One client needs a poster but offers only bags of rice. Zainab already has enough food and needs money for data, transport, and school materials.

prompts.prompt: Why might direct barter be inconvenient for Zainab?
prompts.expected_answer: She does not need rice; her needs are data, transport and materials.

prompts.prompt: How could payment in money help?
prompts.expected_answer: She can sell the poster for money and spend it on what she needs.

prompts.prompt: What would happen if Zainab could only accept goods that she personally needed?
prompts.expected_answer: She would struggle to find clients whose offers match her needs - double coincidence of wants.

items.extension: Identify another profession that benefits from being paid in money.

items.title: Prices Help Us Compare
items.subtitle: See how expressing values in a common unit makes everyday choices easier.

body.text: Suppose a market displays these prices:
The prices give buyers a common unit for comparing the cost of different goods. Without a common unit, people would have to negotiate how many bags of rice equal one container of oil, and so on.
A price tells you how much money a seller is asking. It does not automatically tell you whether the item is affordable, worthwhile, or fairly priced.

items.title: Build a ₦10,000 Basket
items.subtitle: Practise using money prices to compare options and make spending decisions.

config.mechanic: Learner selects items; remaining balance updates live. Then compares two baskets with different combinations.

items.feedback: Practise adding prices, comparing alternatives, and recognising that a limited budget requires choices.
items.learning_objective: Practise adding prices, comparing alternatives, and recognising that a limited budget requires choices.

items.title: Money Can Wait for Tomorrow
items.subtitle: Explore how holding money allows people to delay spending until they need something.

body.text: Imagine receiving ₦20,000 today but needing to pay for textbooks next week.
You don't have to exchange your current possessions immediately for the textbooks. You can hold the money and spend it when the time comes. This demonstrates money's store-of-value function.
However, money does not preserve purchasing power perfectly. If prices rise, the same amount may buy fewer goods later.
Money makes saving and delayed spending possible, but it does not eliminate the effects of inflation or poor financial decisions.

items.key_takeaway: Money makes trade and economic coordination easier, but having money does not guarantee affordability, financial security, or lasting purchasing power.

groups.title: When Money No Dey Work Well
groups.objective: Recognise that money's usefulness depends on acceptance, trust, and the ability to make payments.

items.title: The Note Nobody Wants
items.subtitle: Explore what happens when people refuse to accept something offered as payment.

body.text: Imagine someone offers to pay for food using a note that the seller believes is counterfeit. The seller refuses it.
Although the buyer has presented something that looks like money, the seller does not trust it as a valid means of payment.
Money's usefulness depends partly on people being able to recognise and accept it within the relevant monetary system.

items.title: Will You Accept This Payment?
items.subtitle: Decide whether different forms of payment are usable in a given transaction.

scenario.narrative: A customer wants to pay for groceries using one of three options: valid cash accepted by the seller; a bank transfer that the seller has not yet received; a suspicious note that the seller believes may be counterfeit.

prompts.prompt: Which payments can safely and reliably complete the purchase?
prompts.expected_answer: Valid cash when accepted; a transfer only after it is verified; never the suspected counterfeit.

items.debrief: Valid cash may complete the transaction when accepted. A transfer should be verified before treating the payment as completed. A suspected counterfeit note should not be treated as valid money.
items.key_takeaway: The appearance of money or a payment claim is not the same as a valid, completed payment.

items.title: Money No Be the Same as Wealth
items.subtitle: Distinguish between the money you hold and the broader resources you own.

body.text: Two people each have ₦100,000 in cash. One also owns productive equipment used to earn income. The other has no additional assets and owes ₦80,000.
Their financial positions are not necessarily equal.
Money is one financial resource. Wealth is broader and includes assets and liabilities. This distinction is explored more deeply in Lesson 2.

items.title: True or False?
items.subtitle: Check whether you can distinguish money's functions from its limitations.

questions.prompt: Money eliminates every difficulty associated with buying and selling.
questions.explanation: Money eases exchange but does not remove scarcity, affordability or trust problems.

questions.prompt: People can use money to compare the prices of different goods.
questions.explanation: Money is a unit of account - a common measure for prices.

questions.prompt: Money always retains the same purchasing power over time.
questions.explanation: Rising prices can reduce what a given amount buys.

questions.prompt: Something that looks like money must automatically be accepted as payment.
questions.explanation: Acceptance depends on validity and trust within the payment system.

questions.prompt: Money and wealth mean exactly the same thing.
questions.explanation: Wealth includes assets and liabilities, not just money held.

items.title: The System Still Needs Rules
items.subtitle: Understand why reliable payment systems and safeguards matter to everyday transactions.

body.text: Modern money works within financial and legal systems. People rely on payment providers, banks, merchants, and public institutions to support transactions.
When payments are delayed, records are inaccurate, or fraud occurs, people may struggle to complete ordinary purchases.
This is why payment verification, reliable records, and protection against fraud matter.

items.key_takeaway: Money is powerful because it helps people exchange value, but reliable transactions also depend on trust, acceptance, and functioning systems.

groups.title: Back to the Market
groups.objective: Apply the lesson's concepts to realistic decisions and distinguish between barter and monetary exchange.
groups.group_takeaway: Money is useful because it simplifies exchange, provides a common unit for prices, and allows people to hold purchasing power for later use.

items.title: Two Markets, One Mission
items.subtitle: Compare how a buyer obtains the same item through barter and through money.

body.text: You need a schoolbag. In Market A, you must find a seller willing to exchange the bag for something you own. In Market B, you can buy the bag with money the seller accepts.
Neither situation guarantees that the bag will be available or affordable. However, Market B removes the need for the seller to want the particular item you own.
Money changes how people coordinate exchanges; it does not remove every constraint.

items.title: Choose Your Route
items.subtitle: Solve the same purchasing problem using two different exchange methods.

rounds.label: Barter
rounds.task: Obtain a schoolbag by identifying an acceptable item and negotiating.

rounds.label: Money
rounds.task: Obtain the schoolbag using money: check price and available budget.

debrief_questions: Which route made the cost easier to compare?
What problems remained in both rounds?

items.feedback: Debrief highlights that money reduces negotiation and eases price comparison but price, availability and budget remain constraints.

items.title: What If Everybody Wants the Same Thing?
items.subtitle: Investigate how scarcity and changing demand can affect transactions even when money exists.

body.text: Imagine a shop has only five power banks left, but twenty students want to buy one.
Money makes it easier for the shop to state a price and receive payment. It does not create additional power banks.
The shop may sell out, increase its price, or limit the quantity each person can buy.
Money facilitates transactions, but the availability of goods and services still matters.

items.title: The Last Five Power Banks
items.subtitle: Decide how buyers and sellers might respond when demand exceeds available supply.

scenario.narrative: Twenty students want power banks, but the shop has only five.

prompts.prompt: Predict what could happen if the price remains unchanged.
Predict what could happen if the seller raises the price.
Predict what could happen if the shop receives another shipment.
Predict what could happen if some students buy a different product.

items.key_takeaway: Connects money's role to prices, supply, demand and scarcity without confusing them.

items.title: Explain It to Your Friend
items.subtitle: Demonstrate that you understand why money is useful without relying on memorised definitions.
items.task: Your friend asks: 'If people can exchange things directly, why do we even need money?' Prepare a short explanation.

rubric.description: Explains why barter can be difficult
Explains how money makes exchange easier
States why money does not solve every economic problem

items.notes: Learners record a short response or assemble an explanation using key concepts; the app checks that the central ideas are present.

groups.title: The Ultimate Market Test
groups.objective: Combine the lesson's concepts in a practical scenario and demonstrate independent reasoning.

items.title: You Are Running the Market
items.subtitle: Apply what you have learned to help a small community exchange goods more effectively.

body.text: A community has five traders: a farmer selling yams, a fish seller, a tailor, a phone repairer, and a food vendor.
They regularly struggle to exchange goods because each person wants different things. The community asks you to propose a better way to organise their transactions.
Your task: recommend a system that would make exchanges easier, explain how it would work, and identify at least one problem it would not automatically solve.

items.title: Fix the Trade
items.subtitle: Design a workable exchange system and justify your choices using the lesson's concepts.
items.task: Recommend a system that makes exchange easier for the five traders and justify it.

rubric.description: Appropriate use of the three functions of money

stages.title: Identify the problem
stages.prompt: Explain why direct barter may fail when traders have different needs.

stages.title: Propose a solution
stages.prompt: Explain how a commonly accepted form of money could help the traders complete transactions.

stages.title: Explain the benefits
stages.prompt: Identify how your solution supports buying and selling, comparing prices, and holding purchasing power for future purchases.

stages.title: Identify a limitation
stages.prompt: Explain why your system cannot guarantee that every trader will have the goods they need or that everyone will be able to afford them.

items.title: So, Why We Need Money?
items.subtitle: Consolidate the main lesson before moving to the next concept.

body.text: Money helps people exchange goods and services without needing to find someone who wants exactly what they offer.
It provides a common way to express prices and allows people to hold purchasing power for future spending.
But money does not create unlimited resources, guarantee fair prices, or preserve purchasing power forever.
Money makes economic exchange easier. Understanding how it works helps you make better sense of everyday financial life.

final_quiz.title: Money Matter - Have You Got the Point?
final_quiz.subtitle: Test your understanding of barter, the functions of money, and the problems money helps solve.

questions.explanation: Direct barter requires both parties to want what the other offers.

questions.prompt: Which situation best demonstrates money's role as a medium of exchange?

options.text: A person compares the prices of two phones.
A person keeps money for next month's expenses.
A customer pays a trader for a bag of rice.
A trader records the price of a bag of rice.

questions.explanation: Money is being used to complete a purchase.

questions.prompt: A student compares a ₦15,000 bag with a ₦20,000 bag. Which function of money helps the student compare their prices?
questions.explanation: Money provides a common unit for expressing and comparing prices.

questions.prompt: A person keeps ₦50,000 for three months. During that period, the prices of many goods rise. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The money must buy exactly the same quantity of goods.
Money can no longer be used as a medium of exchange.

questions.explanation: Rising prices can reduce the quantity of goods and services a given amount of money can buy.

questions.prompt: Why can money make exchange easier than barter?

options.text: It guarantees that every product will be affordable.
It allows people to sell to one person and buy from another.
It ensures that every seller accepts every possible payment method.

questions.explanation: Money separates the act of selling from the act of buying, reducing the need for a direct match between the parties' wants.

questions.prompt: A trader has plenty of goods but cannot obtain a product that nobody in the market is selling. What does this illustrate?

Barter is always more efficient than money.
Prices cannot exist without physical cash.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes money?

options.text: Money and wealth are identical concepts.
Money is generally accepted for payments and performs important economic functions.
Money always maintains its purchasing power.

questions.explanation: Money can take different forms, and its economic role is defined by its functions within the relevant system.

questions.prompt: A designer creates a logo for a business. The business pays the designer in money, which the designer later uses to buy food from another seller. What advantage does this demonstrate?

options.text: The designer must trade directly with the food seller.
Money allows separate transactions with different people.
Money removes the need for goods and services.
Money guarantees that the designer will become wealthy.

questions.explanation: Money allows the designer to exchange a service for money and use that money in a separate transaction.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not one of money's three traditional functions?
questions.explanation: Money helps facilitate exchange and economic calculation, but it does not create unlimited resources.

questions.prompt: In your own words, explain one problem associated with barter, how money helps solve it, and one limitation of money.
questions.model_answer: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants, so finding a partner is hard. Money lets you sell to one person and buy from another. Money does not create goods, guarantee affordability, or keep its purchasing power if prices rise.

Explains how money makes exchange easier

core_definition.intuitive_title: The Thing Everybody Can Use to Exchange Value
core_definition.formal_definition: Money is an asset or instrument generally accepted as payment for goods and services and for settling debts within an economy. Its major functions are to serve as a medium of exchange, a unit of account, and a store of value.
core_definition.why_it_matters: Money is not merely cash or the balance displayed in an app. Its economic role comes from how it is used and accepted within a monetary system.

Income is money received. An expense is money spent or owed for goods, services, or obligations.

items.title: Money Enter, Money Comot
items.subtitle: Separate incoming money from spending so you can understand your cash flow.

body.text: Examples of money coming in: wages, business sales, allowances, gifts, and freelance payments.
Examples of money going out: transport, food, data, rent contributions, subscriptions, and debt repayments.
A cash-flow record helps show whether you are spending less than, equal to, or more than you receive.

items.title: Sort Am Correctly
items.subtitle: Practise classifying common transactions as money in or money out.

cards.label: Transport fare
cards.feedback: Spending on transport is an expense.

cards.label: Repayment
cards.feedback: Repaying a debt is money going out.

config.extra_feedback: Borrowing creates money available now but also creates an obligation to repay.

items.feedback: Feedback explains each classification and clarifies that borrowing creates money available now but also an obligation to repay.

items.title: In or Out?
items.subtitle: Check whether you can classify everyday financial transactions accurately.

questions.prompt: You receive ₦15,000 for designing a flyer.
questions.explanation: Payment received for work is income.

questions.prompt: You pay ₦2,000 for transport.
questions.explanation: Money spent on a service is an expense.

questions.prompt: You borrow ₦10,000 from a friend.
questions.explanation: Cash comes in, but a repayment obligation is also created - borrowed money is not income.

questions.prompt: A customer promises to pay next week but has not paid yet.
questions.explanation: A promise to pay is not cash received.

groups.title: Small Spending, Big Picture
groups.objective: Use a simple record to see where money goes.

items.title: Where Did the ₦500 Go?
items.subtitle: Notice how repeated small purchases can add up across a week or month.

body.text: One small purchase may feel unimportant, but repeated purchases can become a meaningful part of your spending.
For example, spending ₦500 every day for 20 days totals ₦10,000.
The goal is not to shame small treats. It is to make spending visible so you can choose deliberately.

items.title: The Data-and-Snack Mystery
items.subtitle: Use a fictional spending record to identify patterns without judging the person.

scenario.narrative: Femi receives ₦25,000 for the week. His record shows transport ₦6,000, lunch ₦7,000, data ₦3,000, snacks ₦4,000, and other purchases ₦3,000.

prompts.prompt: How much did he spend?
How much remains?
Which categories might he want to review?

items.debrief: Learners should identify patterns and trade-offs, not assume that every optional expense is automatically wrong.

items.title: A Record Beats Guesswork
items.subtitle: Learn why writing down transactions is more reliable than relying on memory.

body.text: A simple record can include date, item or purpose, amount, and category.
You can use a notebook, spreadsheet, or a trusted app. The tool matters less than keeping the record consistently.
Record enough information to make decisions, but protect private financial information.

items.title: Find the Leak, Keep the Joy
items.subtitle: Choose one spending pattern to adjust while preserving an expense that matters to you.
items.task: Review a fictional week's spending and select one change that frees up money.

rubric.description: States the amount the change frees up
Explains why the change is realistic

items.notes: There is no single correct category to cut; the reasoning must fit the person's priorities.

contents.title: Your Financial Snapshot
contents.objective: Build a simple picture of money available, financial obligations, and current resources without confusing cash flow with overall financial position.

groups.title: Balance Is Not the Whole Story
groups.objective: Separate available money from committed money.

items.title: Your App Says ₦40k - Now What?
items.subtitle: Understand why a balance must be considered alongside upcoming bills and obligations.

body.text: A person may have ₦40,000 available today but owe ₦15,000 for a bill tomorrow.
The balance alone does not show what portion is already needed for a commitment.
A financial snapshot asks what you have, what you owe, and what payments are coming soon.

items.title: Money You Have vs. Money Already Spoken For
items.subtitle: Separate money currently available from money you have committed to a specific purpose.

body.text: If ₦10,000 is set aside for rent, treating it as free spending money can cause a shortfall.
A planned amount is not necessarily a separate legal account; it can simply be a clear personal allocation.
Knowing your commitments helps you avoid accidentally spending money needed for essential payments.

items.title: The Real Available Balance
items.subtitle: Calculate what remains after subtracting near-term commitments from available money.

inputs.label: Transport and food needed before payday

outputs.label: Not yet allocated to these listed needs

items.feedback: Remind learners to include other known obligations before deciding that the remainder is freely spendable.

groups.title: What You Own and What You Owe
groups.objective: Build a simple picture of what you own and owe.

items.title: Your Money Story Has Two Sides
items.subtitle: Recognise that a financial position includes resources as well as obligations.

body.text: Something of value that a person owns or controls.
A debt or other financial obligation.
The value of assets minus liabilities. It is a snapshot and does not replace a cash-flow plan.

items.title: Two People, Same Salary
items.subtitle: Compare two fictional financial situations to see why income alone cannot describe financial health.

scenario.narrative: Scenario A: Ada earns ₦120,000 monthly, has ₦80,000 in savings, and owes ₦10,000. Scenario B: Bode earns ₦120,000 monthly, has ₦20,000 in savings, and owes ₦150,000.

prompts.prompt: Do they earn the same amount?
Are their current obligations the same?
What else would you need to know before judging their overall situation?

items.debrief: The figures show different snapshots, but a full assessment would also consider expenses, assets, repayment terms, dependants, and income stability.

items.title: Build a Mini Money Snapshot
items.subtitle: Organise a fictional person's listed resources and obligations into a clear summary.
items.task: Assets: savings ₦30,000; laptop estimated resale value ₦70,000. Liabilities: unpaid loan ₦25,000. Calculate simplified net worth.

rubric.description: Notes that estimated value may differ from sale price and that net worth is not immediately spendable

items.notes: Expected: ₦30,000 + ₦70,000 - ₦25,000 = ₦75,000. Debrief: resale value is an estimate; net worth does not mean all assets are immediately spendable.

final_quiz.title: Read Your Money
final_quiz.subtitle: Check whether you can distinguish income, spending, available cash, assets, and liabilities.

questions.prompt: You receive ₦8,000 from a customer for completed work.
questions.explanation: Payment received for work is income.

questions.prompt: You have ₦20,000 but must pay a ₦7,000 bill today. Ignoring other commitments, what remains after the bill?
What is a liability?
If assets are ₦100,000 and liabilities are ₦35,000, what is net worth?
Why is tracking spending useful?
questions.model_answer: It makes patterns visible and supports informed decisions.

final_quiz.note: Source labels this 'Content 1 End-of-Content Quiz' but places it after Content 2 and covers both contents. Attached to CT2 with covers_contents. See SC-03.

lesson_assessment.reason: Module capstone and in-group challenges may suffice.

Build a simple picture of money available, financial obligations, and current resources without confusing cash flow with overall financial position.

lessons.title: Budgeting Without Punishing Yourself

contents.title: Build a Budget That Fits Real Life
contents.objective: Create a realistic plan for allocating expected income to needs, wants, commitments, and future priorities.

groups.title: Tell Every Naira Its Job
groups.objective: Create a realistic plan for allocating expected income.

items.title: A Budget Is a Plan, Not a Prison
items.subtitle: Understand a budget as a flexible plan for deciding what your money needs to do.

body.text: A budget estimates money coming in and assigns money to spending, saving, and obligations.
It helps you compare priorities before money disappears through unplanned purchases.
A useful budget should reflect real income, real costs, and reasonable flexibility.

items.title: Start with What Is Certain
items.subtitle: Build a budget around realistic income rather than money you merely hope to receive.

body.text: List reliable income first.
If income varies, use a cautious estimate based on what is reasonably likely, then adjust when money actually arrives.
Avoid making essential commitments based only on uncertain future income.

items.title: Budget Builder: Naija Edition
items.subtitle: Allocate a fictional monthly income across expenses and priorities.

validation_feedback: alignment with the learner's stated priorities

items.feedback: No universal percentage split is prescribed. Feedback focuses on coverage, realism, and alignment with priorities.

items.title: Can This Budget Survive?
items.subtitle: Identify whether a sample budget fits within the person's available income.

questions.prompt: Income: ₦80,000. Planned expenses and allocations: ₦30,000 + ₦18,000 + ₦12,000 + ₦10,000 + ₦15,000. Does the plan fit the income?
questions.explanation: The total is ₦85,000, which exceeds ₦80,000 by ₦5,000. Revise categories or find a realistic way to increase income - do not ignore the difference.

groups.title: Needs, Wants, and Real-Life Trade-Offs
groups.objective: Prioritise when money cannot cover everything.

items.title: Your Budget Must Know Your Life
items.subtitle: Recognise that essential costs differ across people's circumstances.

body.text: A student living at home may have different costs from a student renting a room.
A person supporting family members may have obligations that another person does not.
A budget should be judged by whether it fits the person's actual circumstances, not by copying somebody else's spending plan.

items.title: The Month Has Too Many Bills
items.subtitle: Prioritise expenses when the available money cannot cover every planned purchase.

scenario.narrative: Nneka has ₦45,000 available. She needs transport ₦10,000, food ₦15,000, a required school payment ₦12,000, data ₦4,000, and wants new headphones costing ₦9,000.

prompts.prompt: What is the total of the listed costs?
prompts.expected_answer: ₦50,000, which exceeds the available amount by ₦5,000

prompts.prompt: Which obligations are time-sensitive?
What options could Nneka consider?

items.debrief: Identify priorities, consider lower-cost alternatives, and avoid assuming every situation has an easy solution.

items.title: Make the Numbers Behave
items.subtitle: Revise an over-budget plan and explain the trade-offs behind each change.
items.task: Reduce the sample plan by at least ₦5,000 without removing a mandatory payment.

rubric.description: Does not remove a mandatory payment
Explains why the changes are feasible

items.notes: Options include delaying headphones, choosing a cheaper data plan if suitable, or other realistic adjustments.

contents.title: When the Plan Meets Reality
contents.objective: Respond constructively when actual income or expenses differ from the original plan.

groups.title: Life No Dey Follow Spreadsheet
groups.objective: Respond constructively when actual income or expenses differ from the plan.

items.title: The Unexpected ₦6,000
items.subtitle: See why a budget needs room for changing costs and surprises.

body.text: You planned to spend ₦8,000 on transport, but fares and extra trips make the total ₦14,000.
The original budget was a plan based on estimates, not a guarantee that reality would follow it.
When costs change, review the plan and update it instead of pretending the original numbers are still correct.

items.title: Budget Shock Simulator
items.subtitle: Adjust a budget after one cost rises or income falls.

config.start_state: A balanced sample budget (AUTHOR_TODO: supply category amounts)
config.learner_action: Reallocate categories so total <= available income

items.feedback: Feedback rewards clear priorities and realistic adjustments rather than one fixed answer.

items.title: Review, Don't Give Up
items.subtitle: Learn to treat a budget miss as information for improving the next plan.

body.text: Compare planned amounts with actual spending.
Ask whether the difference came from an inaccurate estimate, an unexpected event, or a deliberate choice.
Use what you learn to update next month's plan.

items.title: Plan vs. Reality
items.subtitle: Practise diagnosing why actual spending differs from a budget.

questions.prompt: A medical expense appears unexpectedly.
questions.explanation: Not predictable in the original plan.

questions.prompt: You repeatedly budget too little for transport.
questions.explanation: A repeated gap shows the estimate itself is wrong.

questions.prompt: You choose to spend more on a planned celebration.
questions.explanation: A deliberate choice - review its effect on other priorities.

questions.prompt: Your income is lower than expected.
questions.explanation: Recalculate the plan using the income actually available.

final_quiz.title: Budget Without Blind Spots
final_quiz.subtitle: Demonstrate that you can build, check, and adjust a realistic budget.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a budget?
questions.model_answer: To plan how available income will be allocated.

questions.prompt: A person earns ₦60,000 and plans to spend ₦52,000. How much remains before any unlisted costs?
Why should uncertain income be treated cautiously?
questions.model_answer: It may not arrive when expected or may be lower than hoped.

questions.prompt: What should you do when actual costs differ from estimates?
questions.model_answer: Review the difference and update the plan.

questions.prompt: A budget is automatically bad if one month does not go to plan.
questions.explanation: It should be reviewed and adjusted.

lesson_assessment.reason: Module capstone and in-group challenges may suffice.

goals.statement: Create a realistic plan for allocating expected income to needs, wants, commitments, and future priorities.
Respond constructively when actual income or expenses differ from the original plan.

chapters.title: Saving Is a Habit, Not Leftovers

lessons.title: How to Start Saving When Money Is Tight

contents.title: Pay Yourself First - Even If It Is Small
contents.objective: Understand saving, choose a realistic starting amount, and make saving part of a repeatable routine.

groups.title: Don't Wait for Plenty Money
groups.objective: Understand saving and choose a realistic starting amount.

items.title: Saving No Be Competition
items.subtitle: Recognise that a useful saving habit is about consistency and purpose, not comparing amounts with other people.

body.text: Setting aside some available money for future use rather than spending it now.
The amount that is realistic depends on income, essential costs, obligations, and circumstances.
A small, repeatable amount may be a better starting point than an ambitious target that cannot be maintained.

items.title: Give Tomorrow Something
items.subtitle: Connect saving today with a future expense or goal.

body.text: Saving can support planned purchases, education costs, future bills, or an emergency reserve.
A clear purpose makes it easier to decide how much to save and when the money may be used.
Savings should not be confused with money that must be spent on immediate essentials.

items.title: Pick a Realistic Starting Point
items.subtitle: Choose a saving amount that fits a fictional person's income and obligations.

config.scenario: A learner receives ₦20,000 monthly, contributes ₦12,000 to essential costs, spends ₦5,000 on transport and data, and has other small necessary costs.
config.options: AUTHOR_TODO: several saving amounts (e.g. very small / moderate / ambitious) with trade-off text
config.learner_task: Choose an amount and explain the trade-off.

items.feedback: The right amount depends on the full situation; no universal savings rate is imposed.

items.title: Savings or Leftovers?
items.subtitle: Distinguish intentional saving from whatever happens to remain by chance.

questions.prompt: You set aside ₦1,000 immediately after receiving income.
questions.explanation: Setting money aside first is deliberate saving.

questions.prompt: You plan to save but spend everything before month-end.
questions.explanation: No money was actually set aside.

questions.prompt: You revise your savings amount because essential costs rise.
questions.explanation: A reasonable adjustment may be appropriate when circumstances change.

groups.title: Make the Habit Easy
groups.objective: Build a repeatable saving routine.

items.title: Small, Then Repeat
items.subtitle: Use a manageable routine to reduce the effort needed to save consistently.

body.text: Choose a time or trigger, such as the day income arrives.
Choose a realistic amount and a safe place to keep it.
Review the habit periodically and adjust when circumstances change.

items.title: The First ₦5,000
items.subtitle: Compare two saving routines and decide which is more sustainable for the person.

scenario.narrative: Scenario A: Kunle plans to save ₦5,000 every week but often needs that money for transport and food. Scenario B: If his budget supports it, Kunle starts with ₦1,000 weekly and reviews the amount after a month.

prompts.prompt: Which plan is more realistic based on the information given?
What additional information would help?

items.debrief: Scenario B may be easier to maintain, but learners should use the person's actual budget rather than assume one plan always wins.

items.title: Design Your Saving Trigger
items.subtitle: Create a simple saving routine linked to a predictable event.
items.task: Complete: 'When ______ happens, I will set aside ______ for ______.' Identify one obstacle and a backup plan.
items.notes: The app checks the plan is specific, realistic, and connected to a purpose.

contents.title: Make Saving Easier to Repeat
contents.objective: Use goals, separation, and review routines to make savings easier to protect.

groups.title: Name the Money
groups.objective: Use goals, separation, and review routines to protect savings.

items.title: Money with a Mission
items.subtitle: Use clear labels to distinguish savings for different purposes.

body.text: A person may save separately for school materials, a device, a planned trip, or emergencies.
Labels can help prevent money intended for one purpose from being spent casually on another.
Keep the system simple enough to maintain and avoid unnecessary fees or complexity.

items.title: Split the Savings
items.subtitle: Allocate a fictional amount among several goals and review the trade-offs.
items.feedback: Feedback focuses on urgency, deadlines, and personal priorities rather than a single correct split.

items.title: Make Saving Visible
items.subtitle: Track progress so that small contributions add up to a measurable result.

body.text: A simple progress record can show the target, current amount, remaining amount, and next step.
Progress tracking can motivate learners, but missing a target should trigger a review rather than shame.
Protect account credentials and avoid sharing sensitive financial details publicly.

items.title: Which Habit Helps?
items.subtitle: Choose practical habits that make a saving plan easier to maintain.

questions.prompt: Set a realistic amount and review it.
questions.explanation: Realistic and reviewed plans are easier to sustain.

questions.prompt: Save money needed for an urgent essential bill without a plan to cover it.
questions.explanation: It may leave an essential obligation unpaid.

questions.prompt: Track progress toward a clear goal.
questions.explanation: Visible progress supports consistency.

questions.prompt: Compare your savings with an influencer's without knowing their circumstances.
questions.explanation: You do not know their income, obligations or support.

lessons.title: Emergency Funds and Unexpected Expenses

contents.title: The Difference Between an Emergency and a Want
contents.objective: Recognise unexpected essential costs and understand why a financial buffer can reduce pressure.

groups.title: When Life Sends an Invoice
groups.objective: Recognise unexpected essential costs and why a buffer reduces pressure.

items.title: The Phone Just Spoilt
items.subtitle: Consider how an unplanned but necessary expense can disrupt a person's budget.

body.text: A phone needed for work suddenly needs repair.
The expense was not part of the original plan, but ignoring it may affect income or essential communication.
A financial buffer can help absorb some unexpected costs without immediately relying on borrowing.

items.title: Emergency, Need, or Want?
items.subtitle: Classify expenses by urgency and importance rather than by how strongly someone desires them.

body.text: An unexpected event requiring timely attention.
Something important for health, safety, basic living, or a significant obligation.
May be enjoyable or valuable but can often be delayed without serious harm.
Context matters: replacing a phone may be urgent for a delivery worker but less urgent for someone with a working alternative.

items.title: Three Problems, One Wallet
items.subtitle: Prioritise competing expenses using urgency, consequences, and available alternatives.

scenario.narrative: A learner has ₦8,000 available. Their work shoes are damaged, a non-essential game is on sale, and transport is needed to attend an exam.

prompts.prompt: Which expense is time-sensitive?
What alternatives exist?
What information would change your decision?

items.debrief: Transport to the exam is likely a high priority; the damaged shoes depend on safety and available alternatives; the game can usually wait.

items.title: Emergency or Just Urgent Feeling?
items.subtitle: Test whether you can distinguish a genuine financial priority from a tempting purchase.

questions.prompt: Essential medicine is needed today.
questions.explanation: Treat as urgent and seek appropriate professional guidance as relevant.

questions.prompt: A limited-time discount on a fashionable item ends tonight.
questions.explanation: Not automatically an emergency; the deadline is the seller's, not yours.

questions.prompt: Transport money is needed to attend a required exam.
questions.explanation: It has a fixed deadline and a serious consequence if missed.

questions.prompt: A required work tool breaks and prevents earning income.
questions.explanation: Depends on alternatives and consequences for income.

groups.title: Borrowing Is Not the Only Backup
groups.objective: Weigh options other than borrowing.

items.title: Pause Before You Borrow
items.subtitle: Consider the cost and consequences of borrowing to cover an unexpected expense.

body.text: Borrowing may provide immediate funds, but it can add interest, fees, repayment dates, and pressure on future income.
Before borrowing, consider the urgency, amount required, repayment ability, and safer alternatives.
Avoid high-pressure offers that hide the total repayment amount or demand sensitive information.

items.title: Emergency Options Check
items.subtitle: Compare possible responses to a fictional unexpected bill.

config.learner_task: For each option, identify benefits, risks, and missing information.

items.feedback: Options depend on the situation; no option is universally best.

contents.title: Build Your Safety Cushion
contents.objective: Set a realistic emergency-fund target and develop a gradual plan to build it.

groups.title: Start with a First Buffer
groups.objective: Set a realistic emergency-fund target and a plan to build it.

items.title: Your First Safety Net
items.subtitle: Set an initial target that is useful and achievable for your circumstances.

body.text: Money kept for unexpected necessary expenses or income disruption.
A first target can be modest and later grow as income and circumstances allow.
There is no single target that suits everyone; essential expenses, income stability, dependants, and available support all matter.

items.title: How Big Is Your Buffer?
items.subtitle: Estimate a starter emergency target using essential costs and personal circumstances.

outputs.label: Periods needed at each contribution amount

config.note: Show timelines for several contribution amounts; explain that a starter buffer is a beginning, not a guarantee.

items.feedback: Explains that a starter buffer is a beginning, not a guarantee against every emergency.

items.title: Keep It Reachable, Keep It Separate
items.subtitle: Choose a safe, accessible way to keep emergency savings apart from everyday spending.

body.text: Emergency money should be accessible when needed and held somewhere reasonably safe.
Compare access, reliability, fees, and relevant protections before choosing a financial service.
Avoid putting essential emergency money into volatile investments or arrangements that may prevent timely access.

items.title: Build the Backup Plan
items.subtitle: Create a step-by-step plan for starting and gradually growing an emergency reserve.
items.task: Specify an initial target, contribution amount, schedule, what qualifies as an emergency, and how you will replenish the reserve after using it.

rubric.description: Initial target, contribution amount and schedule specified
Fits budget; does not depend on uncertain income

final_quiz.title: Ready for the Unexpected?
final_quiz.subtitle: Check your understanding of emergency spending and financial buffers.

questions.prompt: What is an emergency fund for?
questions.model_answer: Unexpected necessary expenses or income disruption.

questions.prompt: Every discounted purchase is an emergency.
questions.explanation: A discount is a sales tactic, not an emergency.

questions.prompt: Why might borrowing create future pressure?
questions.model_answer: Repayments, interest, and fees reduce future available income.

questions.explanation: Circumstances differ: essentials, income stability, dependants and support.

questions.prompt: Where should emergency money generally be kept?
questions.model_answer: Somewhere reasonably safe and accessible, chosen with costs and reliability in mind.

lessons.title: Needs, Wants, and Impulse Spending

contents.title: Before You Tap Buy
contents.objective: Identify needs and wants, pause before impulse purchases, and assess a purchase against priorities.

groups.title: Want Am or Need Am?
groups.objective: Identify needs and wants and pause before impulse purchases.

items.title: Your Cart Is Not Your Priority List
items.subtitle: Separate what is necessary from what is desirable in a specific situation.

body.text: A need supports essential living, safety, health, work, or an important obligation.
A want can improve comfort or enjoyment but may be delayed or replaced.
The same item can be a need in one situation and a want in another.

items.title: One Budget, Four Choices
items.subtitle: Rank a fictional set of expenses according to urgency and personal circumstances.

scenario.narrative: A learner has ₦12,000. Choices include food for the next few days, transport to work, a phone case, and a new game.

choices: Food for the next few days

prompts.prompt: Rank the four choices and explain your ranking.
What extra information might change it?

items.debrief: The exercise is about reasoning and context, not labelling every enjoyable purchase as bad.

items.title: The Real Cost Is More Than the Price
items.subtitle: Consider what a purchase uses up besides the money paid at checkout.

body.text: A purchase also uses money that could have gone toward another goal.
Recurring payments can continue after the excitement of the first purchase fades.
Check total cost, maintenance, delivery, fees, and future commitments where relevant.

items.title: The 24-Hour Pause
items.subtitle: Practise delaying non-urgent purchases long enough to reconsider them.

config.setup: A tempting non-essential purchase is shown.
after_pause_questions: Can I afford it without missing a priority?
config.note: The pause is a decision aid, not a rule that must apply to every purchase.

items.feedback: Reveal what the learner's choice led to after a simulated pause.

groups.title: When Your Mood Holds Your Wallet
groups.objective: Recognise emotional triggers and build a personal pause rule.

items.title: Shopping to Change Your Mood
items.subtitle: Notice how boredom, stress, excitement, or disappointment can influence spending.

body.text: People sometimes spend to seek comfort, celebrate, fit in, or escape an unpleasant feeling.
The emotion is real, but a purchase may not solve the underlying problem.
Noticing the trigger creates a chance to choose a response deliberately.

items.title: The Bad-Day Checkout
items.subtitle: Help a fictional learner identify an emotional spending trigger and choose an alternative response.

scenario.narrative: After a stressful day, Sola orders expensive food and buys clothes online even though rent contribution is due.

prompts.prompt: What might have triggered the spending?
Which obligation is affected?
What alternative could Sola try before purchasing?

items.debrief: Suggestions may include a short break, talking to someone, choosing a lower-cost treat, or revisiting the budget after emotions settle.

items.title: Create Your Pause Rule
items.subtitle: Write a simple personal rule for reviewing purchases that are large, emotional, or non-essential.
items.task: Choose a threshold or situation that triggers a pause, list three checks (affordability, priority, total cost), and decide what to do if a check fails.

rubric.description: Affordability, priority and total cost included
States what happens if the purchase fails a check

contents.title: Social Pressure, Deals, and FOMO
contents.objective: Recognise social influence and marketing tactics that can push learners toward unplanned spending.

groups.title: Everybody Is Buying It
groups.objective: Separate personal goals from social pressure.

items.title: Their Lifestyle, Your Wallet
items.subtitle: Recognise how friends and social media can distort spending expectations.

body.text: Posts often show purchases and experiences without showing debt, income, family support, or trade-offs.
Copying someone else's lifestyle without knowing their financial situation can create pressure.
A useful decision is one that fits your priorities and resources, not one that proves you can keep up.

items.title: Whose Goal Is This?
items.subtitle: Identify whether a spending decision reflects a personal goal or external pressure.

questions.prompt: You save for a laptop required for your course.
categories: Personal goal linked to a need
questions.correct: Personal goal linked to a need
questions.explanation: The purchase serves your own need.

questions.prompt: You buy expensive shoes only because friends may mock your old ones.
categories: Personal goal linked to a need
questions.explanation: The motive is external approval.

questions.prompt: You compare prices and decide an item fits your plan.
categories: Personal goal linked to a need
questions.explanation: Comparison against your plan shows deliberate choice.

groups.title: Discount No Mean Free
groups.objective: Evaluate deals and time-limited offers.

items.title: You Saved ₦5,000 - Or Did You?
items.subtitle: Understand why a discount only saves money when the purchase itself makes sense.

body.text: If an item falls from ₦20,000 to ₦15,000, you pay ₦15,000 - you do not receive ₦5,000.
If you did not need the item or cannot afford it, the discount may still lead to unnecessary spending.
Compare the final price with your budget and alternatives, not just the size of the advertised discount.

items.title: The Flash Sale Trap
items.subtitle: Evaluate a time-limited offer without allowing urgency to replace affordability checks.

scenario.narrative: A learner sees headphones discounted from ₦30,000 to ₦22,000. They have ₦25,000 but need ₦18,000 for transport and food before payday.

prompts.prompt: Can the learner pay for the headphones and cover the listed essentials?
What would remain after paying for the headphones?
Is the discount enough reason to buy?

items.debrief: The discounted item is unaffordable within the stated constraints, even though the sale looks attractive.

items.title: Read the Small Print
items.subtitle: Check recurring charges, delivery fees, warranties, and conditions before committing to a purchase.

body.text: A low headline price may exclude delivery, service charges, or required accessories.
Subscriptions can renew automatically, creating future costs.
Before paying, check the total amount, cancellation terms, and whether the seller or service is legitimate.

items.title: Beat the FOMO Clock
items.subtitle: Use a short checklist to decide whether to buy, delay, or walk away from a tempting offer.
items.task: Answer: Do I need or genuinely want it? Can I afford it after essentials? Have I checked the full cost? Would I still buy it without the countdown timer? Then choose buy, delay, or walk away.

rubric.description: Chooses buy, delay, or walk away
Reasoning uses numbers and stated constraints

items.notes: The app rewards evidence-based reasoning, not automatically rejecting every purchase.

lessons.title: Set Financial Goals You Can Actually Reach

contents.title: Turn a Wish into a Plan
contents.objective: Convert vague financial wishes into specific targets with amounts, deadlines, and practical next steps.

groups.title: Wish, Goal, Plan
groups.objective: Convert vague wishes into measurable goals.

items.title: I Want to Save More Is Not a Plan
items.subtitle: Turn a broad intention into a goal that can be measured and acted on.

body.text: Something you would like to happen.
Identifies what you want to achieve, how much it costs, and when you want to achieve it.
Identifies the actions and contributions needed to move toward the target.

items.title: Give the Goal a Number and a Date
items.subtitle: Make a goal specific enough to calculate the amount and time required.

body.text: Example: Save ₦60,000 for a course fee in six months.
If no savings have been set aside, the simple average contribution required is ₦10,000 per month, before considering any fees or changes in cost.
If that amount does not fit the budget, reconsider the deadline, target, or ways to increase available funds.

items.title: Goal Calculator
items.subtitle: Calculate a simple regular contribution needed to reach a target by a chosen date.

config.validation: Flag unrealistic inputs (months <= 0, current > target) and remind that costs, income and timing can change.

items.feedback: Reminds learners that costs, income, and timing can change.

items.title: Goal or Just Vibes?
items.subtitle: Identify which statements contain a measurable financial goal.

questions.prompt: 'I want to be better with money.'
questions.explanation: No amount, deadline or action.

questions.prompt: 'I will save ₦30,000 for textbooks over three months.'
questions.explanation: Has an amount, purpose and deadline.

questions.prompt: 'I will save something someday.'
questions.explanation: No amount and no date.

groups.title: Put the Goals in Order
groups.objective: Order competing goals realistically.

items.title: Not Every Goal Comes First
items.subtitle: Prioritise goals by urgency, importance, cost, and consequences of delay.

body.text: People often have several goals but limited money.
A near-term essential payment may need priority over a discretionary purchase.
Priorities can change when income, responsibilities, or circumstances change.

items.title: The Laptop, the Rent, and the Trip
items.subtitle: Balance several competing goals and explain the consequences of the chosen order.

scenario.narrative: A learner wants to save for a laptop needed for coursework, contribute to rent by a deadline, and take a leisure trip.

prompts.prompt: Rank the goals using urgency, consequences, and available alternatives.

items.debrief: There may be more than one defensible plan, but essential commitments and deadlines must be considered explicitly.

items.title: Build Your Three-Goal Ladder
items.subtitle: Choose three fictional goals and create a realistic order for working toward them.
items.task: For each goal record target amount, deadline, priority, and next action. Explain which goal comes first and what you will do if the budget cannot fund all three at once.

rubric.description: Target, deadline, priority and next action for each goal
Explains why the first goal comes first
Plan if budget cannot fund all three

contents.title: Track Progress Without Giving Up
contents.objective: Monitor progress, respond to setbacks, and revise financial goals when circumstances change.

groups.title: Progress Is Data
groups.objective: Monitor progress and revise goals when circumstances change.

items.title: Small Steps Still Move You
items.subtitle: Use regular progress checks to see whether your plan is working.

body.text: Record how much you have saved and how much remains.
Compare actual contributions with the planned amount.
A slow month does not automatically mean failure; it gives you information to review the plan.

items.title: Progress Tracker
items.subtitle: Update a goal after each contribution and see how the remaining target changes.
items.feedback: Shows progress as both an amount and a proportion of the goal.

items.title: When the Plan Slips
items.subtitle: Revise a goal constructively when income, costs, or deadlines change.

body.text: Possible responses include changing the contribution amount, extending the deadline, reducing the target, or finding a realistic additional source of income.
Do not rely on risky borrowing or unrealistic promises just to preserve an old deadline.
A revised plan is useful when it reflects reality and keeps important priorities protected.

items.title: The Price Went Up
items.subtitle: Adjust a savings goal after the cost of the intended purchase increases.

scenario.narrative: A laptop originally expected to cost ₦180,000 now costs ₦210,000. The learner has saved ₦90,000 and has three months remaining.

prompts.prompt: How much more is needed?
What is the simple monthly contribution required if the deadline stays the same?

items.debrief: Decide whether that contribution is realistic and consider changing the deadline, target, or purchase option if necessary.

items.title: The Honest Goal Review
items.subtitle: Review a goal using actual progress and make one evidence-based adjustment.
items.task: Compare target progress with actual progress, identify the reason for any gap, choose one adjustment, and say how you will check whether it works.

rubric.description: Explains how it will be verified

final_quiz.title: Future You Is Counting on You
final_quiz.subtitle: Demonstrate that you can set a measurable goal, calculate contributions, and adapt when circumstances change.

questions.prompt: What makes a financial goal measurable?
questions.model_answer: A clear target and a way to track progress, usually including an amount and deadline.

questions.prompt: A learner needs ₦24,000 in four months and has nothing saved. What simple monthly contribution is required?
A goal becomes unaffordable after an unexpected cost. Name one reasonable response.
questions.model_answer: Revise the amount, timeline, target, or realistic income plan.

questions.prompt: Why should goals be prioritised?
questions.model_answer: Resources are limited and deadlines or consequences differ.

questions.prompt: Missing one contribution automatically means the goal has failed.
questions.explanation: Review the reason and adjust the plan.

capstone.title: The Month You Must Manage
capstone.subtitle: Use tracking, budgeting, saving, prioritisation, and goal-setting together in one realistic scenario.
capstone.task: Tobi receives ₦90,000 this month. Essential costs include food ₦20,000, transport ₦12,000, a family contribution ₦10,000, and data/work costs ₦6,000. Tobi also wants to save toward a ₦45,000 course fee due in three months. An unexpected ₦5,000 repair is required.

rubric.description: Recognises what is not known (other obligations)
Plan makes progress toward the course fee

stages.prompt: Calculate the listed essential costs and repair cost.
Calculate what remains from ₦90,000 before other unlisted expenses.
Calculate the simple monthly contribution needed for the course fee if Tobi has no existing savings.
Propose a plan that covers the listed costs, makes progress toward the course fee, and leaves a realistic allowance for any other known expenses.
Explain what Tobi should reconsider if the plan does not fit the full budget.

capstone.notes: There is no single perfect budget without knowing all of Tobi's obligations.

evaluation_track.overview: The Evaluation Track measures learner performance across the Learning Track. It is derived from the `assessed: true` nodes (quizzes, challenges, capstone), their concept tags, and the lesson-level goals in each lesson.evaluation block.
evaluation_track.status_note: The syllabus defines WHAT is assessed (quiz at every Group, final quiz per Content, lesson challenges, capstone). Numeric thresholds, weights and formulas below are PROPOSED defaults so the developer has something concrete to build; product/learning team should tune them.

group_quiz.purpose: Check understanding right after the Group

practice_quiz.purpose: Reinforce difficult/misunderstood ideas (High and Very High lessons)

content_final.purpose: Test the whole Content unit; application over recall

lesson_assessment.purpose: Integrated lesson-level task (recommended for High/Very High)

module_capstone.purpose: Combine concepts across the module in one scenario

scoring.auto_graded: single_choice, true_false, numeric, classify -> 1.0 if correct else 0.0 (times question.points)
scoring.rubric_graded: challenge and short_answer: each rubric criterion scored 0-3; score = sum / (3 * criteria_count)
scoring.short_answer_default: key_points coverage ratio; >= 0.67 counts as correct, else partial credit = ratio
scoring.retries: Unlimited retries; first-attempt score is stored separately from best score.
scoring.feedback: Always show question.explanation after each answer (design rule: explanatory feedback, not just correct/wrong).

pass_and_gating.unlock_rule: Next Group unlocks when current Group's items are complete (quiz attempted). Next Content unlocks when the previous Content final quiz is >= content_final_pass. Learners may retry to improve.
pass_and_gating.remediation: If a group quiz score < pass: suggest replaying the relevant slides (by concept tags) and, in High/Very High lessons, offer the practice_quizzes. Practice quizzes never block progress.

mastery_model.unit: concept (ids in glossary.concepts and the `concepts` arrays on slides/widgets/questions)
mastery_model.formula: mastery(concept) = sum(w_a * s_q) / sum(w_a) over the learner's most recent N=8 scored responses tagged with the concept; w_a is the assessment_type weight; s_q in [0,1]
mastery_model.lesson_mastery: weighted mean of mastery over the lesson's concepts, weights = number of tagged questions

goals_and_tasks.goal: A lesson learning goal (lesson.evaluation.goals[]). Each goal links to the assessments that evidence it and has a mastery_threshold. goal_progress = (best weighted score across linked assessments) / threshold, capped at 1.
goals_and_tasks.task: A challenge, lesson_assessment or the Module capstone. Task completion = rubric_score >= challenge_pass. Rubric criteria give the learner specific, actionable feedback.
goals_and_tasks.learner_view: GoalsAndTasksBoard lists each goal with progress bar, each task with status (not started / submitted / passed), and the next recommended item.

concepts.definition: The direct exchange of goods or services for other goods or services without using money as the medium of exchange.
The requirement that two parties to a direct exchange each want what the other offers.
A commonly accepted instrument used to purchase goods and services.
A common measure used to express prices, record obligations, and compare economic values.
Something that allows purchasing power to be transferred from the present into the future, although its real value may change.
When people or businesses concentrate on particular activities or products and obtain other goods and services through exchange.
The condition in which available resources are insufficient to satisfy all wants.
The quantity of goods and services that a given amount of money can buy.
Money is one financial resource; wealth is broader and includes assets and liabilities.
Money's usefulness depends on trust, validity and acceptance within the relevant payment system.
Using money prices as a common unit to compare options within a budget.
Money received from work, business activity, investments, gifts, or other sources. A promise to pay later is not the same as money already received.
Money spent or owed for goods, services, or obligations.
The movement of money into and out of a person's or household's finances over a period.
Something of economic value that a person owns or controls.
A debt or other financial obligation.
The value of assets minus liabilities at a particular point in time.
A plan for allocating expected income to expenses, savings, and other financial priorities over a period.
Setting aside available resources for future use rather than spending them immediately.
Money reserved for unexpected necessary expenses or disruptions to income.
A purchase made with little prior planning, often influenced by immediate desire, emotion, or external pressure.
A defined financial outcome with a target and a way to measure progress; useful goals commonly include an amount and a deadline.
Spending money on one option means giving up the next-best alternative.
How easily an asset can be converted into money available for use.
Some costs are relatively stable while others change with usage or circumstances.
Income that varies in timing or amount and therefore requires cautious planning.
The ability to manage shocks and continue meeting important obligations.
Emotions, habits, social pressure, and marketing cues that can influence spending.
Comparing actual progress with the amount and timing required by a plan.
The importance of an expense depends partly on the person's circumstances, alternatives, and deadlines.
A discount only saves money when the purchase itself is needed and affordable; you still pay the discounted price.
